write.desc: How to read, build and write proofs: the standard proof methods, how the logical shape of a statement (for all, there exists, nested quantifiers, if and only if) gives the skeleton of its proof, and the conventions and pitfalls of writing a proof up, all practised on integers, parity, divisibility and school algebra so the learner is ready for the epsilon proofs to come.

points.name: What a proof is and how to read one
points.what: Understand a proof as a chain of justified steps from stated assumptions and definitions to the claim, and be able to read a short proof line by line, saying at each step what is assumed, what is being shown, and which definition or earlier fact justifies it.
outside: what 'if P then Q' claims: hypothesis and conclusion of an implication

points.name: Direct proof
points.what: Prove 'if P then Q' by assuming P and deducing Q, unpacking definitions such as even, odd and 'a divides b' (for example: the sum of two odd integers is even; if a divides b and b divides c then a divides c).
outside: what 'if P then Q' claims: hypothesis and conclusion of an implication

points.name: Proof-writing conventions
points.what: Write a proof that others can follow: say what is assumed and what is to be shown, introduce and name every variable before using it, put words between formulas, justify each step, and end with a clear conclusion.

points.name: Proving 'for all' statements: take an arbitrary element
points.what: Prove a statement 'for all x in S, P(x)' by letting x be an arbitrary element of S, using only what is known about every element of S, and showing P(x); understand why checking examples is not enough.
outside: the quantifier 'for all' with an explicit domain

points.name: Proving 'there exists' statements: produce a witness
points.what: Prove 'there exists x with P(x)' by naming a specific x and checking that it satisfies P(x), and see that the witness is chosen, not assumed.

points.name: Using hypotheses that contain quantifiers
points.what: Use a hypothesis 'for all x, P(x)' by applying it to any particular object you need, and use a hypothesis 'there exists x with P(x)' by giving that object a new name you do not get to choose, keeping track of which objects are fixed and which are arbitrary.

points.name: Proving statements with nested quantifiers
points.what: Turn a statement such as 'for every x there exists y such that for every z ...' into the skeleton of its proof ('Let x be arbitrary. Choose y = ... Let z be arbitrary. Then ...'), with the choice of y allowed to depend on x but not on z; this is exactly the shape of the epsilon proofs to come.
outside: nested quantifiers and why their order matters

points.name: Scratch work versus the final write-up
points.what: Work backwards in scratch work from what is wanted to discover what to choose or assume, then write the final proof forwards from the hypotheses, so the write-up never starts from the conclusion.

points.name: Disproving a statement with a counterexample
points.what: Show a universal statement is false by exhibiting one object for which it fails, check that the counterexample really satisfies the hypotheses and violates the conclusion, and see that this is proving the negated, existential statement.
outside: negating quantified statements ('not for all' becomes 'there exists ... not')

points.name: Proof by contrapositive
points.what: Prove 'if P then Q' by proving 'if not Q then not P', and recognise when this is easier (for example: if n squared is even then n is even).
outside: the contrapositive of an implication and its equivalence to the implication

points.name: Proof by contradiction
points.what: Prove a statement by assuming its negation and deriving something impossible, as in the irrationality of the square root of 2 and the infinitude of the primes, and state the negated assumption correctly at the start.
outside: negating statements, including implications and quantified statements

points.name: Proof by cases
points.what: Split a proof into cases that together cover every possibility (such as n even or n odd, or the possible remainders mod 3), prove the claim in each case, and use 'without loss of generality' only when the cases are truly symmetric.
outside: the connective 'or' and when an 'or' statement is true

points.name: Proving 'if and only if' statements
points.what: Prove 'P if and only if Q' by proving both directions separately, labelled clearly, and recognise when a chain of reversible equivalences can be used instead and when it cannot.
outside: 'if and only if' and the converse of an implication

points.name: Non-constructive existence and uniqueness proofs
points.what: Prove that something exists without exhibiting it (for example by contradiction or by cases), and prove uniqueness by assuming two objects with the property and showing they are equal.

points.name: Common errors in proofs
points.what: Recognise and avoid the usual mistakes: assuming what is to be proved, proving only an example of a universal claim, proving the converse instead of the statement, reusing a variable that is already fixed, and letting a chosen value depend on something chosen later.
outside: the converse of an implication and why it differs from the implication
